lead: A turbine, compressor, nozzle and boiler all do the same accounting: energy in plus heat added equals energy out plus work delivered. Because mass crosses the boundary, energy per kg is enthalpy, not internal energy. Written once and with terms struck out per device, this equation answers exam questions on nozzles, turbines, throttles, condensers and pumps. It is the working tool of power plants, refrigerators and air-conditioners.
prereq: You need: the energy balance of Chapter 2.1, enthalpy and flow work from Chapter 2.2, and the control volume idea from Unit 1, Systems, Properties and Zeroth Law.

sections.h3: The control volume and the four assumptions

blocks.text: An open system lets mass cross its boundary. A fixed region in space is a control volume: a turbine casing, a compressor, a radiator, a pipe.
The mass flow rate ṁ is the mass crossing a section each second, in kg/s.

blocks.where: ρ is density in kg/m³, A is the cross-sectional area in m², V is the velocity in m/s, and v = 1/ρ is the specific volume in m³/kg.

items: Steady state. Nothing inside changes with time; mass in equals mass out, ṁ₁ = ṁ₂ = ṁ, and properties at a fixed point stay constant.
Uniform properties. At each section every fluid element has the same h, V and z.
Negligible storage. Energy held by the control volume does not change, so it never appears in the balance.
q and w are per unit mass. They are in kJ/kg and are the only energy crossings besides the flowing mass.

blocks.text: Energy in equals energy out, per kg of fluid:
h₁ + V₁²/2000 + gz₁/1000 + q = h₂ + V₂²/2000 + gz₂/1000 + w
blocks.where: h is specific enthalpy in kJ/kg; V is velocity in m/s; z is height above a datum in m; g = 9.81 m/s²; q is heat added in kJ/kg, negative if lost; w is shaft work delivered in kJ/kg, negative if work is put in. Subscript 1 is inlet, 2 outlet.

blocks.text: The 2000 and 1000 are unit fixes: V²/2 is J/kg, so V²/2000 is kJ/kg; gz/1000 is also kJ/kg. Adding J/kg to an h in kJ/kg is the classic error.

Why enthalpy, not internal energy? Fluid behind the inlet pushes incoming fluid in, and fluid ahead of the outlet is pushed out. That flow work pv travels with the mass; h = u + pv contains it, so u never appears.
Multiply every term by ṁ for the rate form (kW):
ṁh₁ + ṁV₁²/2000 + ṁgz₁/1000 + Q̇ = ṁh₂ + ṁV₂²/2000 + ṁgz₂/1000 + Ẇ
blocks.where: Q̇ = ṁq is the heat transfer rate in kW and Ẇ = ṁw is the shaft power in kW.

blocks.text: Every device is this one equation with terms removed. Learn the striking out, not eight separate formulas.

items: Nozzle. A short duct that speeds the fluid up. No shaft, negligible heat, no height change: h₁ + V₁²/2000 = h₂ + V₂²/2000. Velocity rises; enthalpy, pressure and temperature fall.
Diffuser. The same duct widening. Velocity falls and enthalpy rises; the equation is identical.
Turbine. Work leaves, the casing is insulated so q ≈ 0, and ΔKE and ΔPE are small beside Δh: w = h₁ − h₂.
Compressor. Work goes in, so w is negative and work input = h₂ − h₁. Again ΔKE and ΔPE are dropped.

Throttle or expansion valve. A plug or part-closed valve. No work, no heat, no time for velocity change: h₁ = h₂, an isenthalpic process. Pressure falls and, for most real gases near room temperature, temperature falls too — the basis of refrigeration; hydrogen and helium are exceptions and warm up.
Boiler, condenser, heater. No shaft work: q = h₂ − h₁.
Heat exchanger. Two streams, no work. For each stream q = h_out − h_in; if insulated, with Δh = h_out − h_in for each stream, ṁ_hot Δh_hot + ṁ_cold Δh_cold = 0.
Pump. A compressor for a liquid, so w_in = h₂ − h₁ ≈ v(p₂ − p₁) because a liquid barely changes volume.

blocks.text: Filling a tank from a supply line is transient: track total mass and total energy. Some syllabi call the steady case SSSF, the tank case USUF (uniform-state uniform-flow).

figure.caption: Fluid enters at section 1 and leaves at section 2 with its three energy terms; heat q crosses inwards and shaft work w outwards. Every device here is this picture with some arrows erased.

spec.title: Steady flow energy balance
spec.aria: Fluid enters a steady control volume carrying enthalpy, kinetic and potential energy, heat crosses the boundary inwards and shaft work leaves, and the fluid exits with its own energy terms.

examples.question: Steam enters a turbine at 2 kg/s with h₁ = 3200 kJ/kg, V₁ = 60 m/s and z₁ = 5 m. It leaves with h₂ = 2600 kJ/kg, V₂ = 150 m/s and z₂ = 0 m. Heat loss from the casing is 20 kJ per kg of steam. Take g = 9.81 m/s². Find the work output per kg of steam and the power output.
steps: Rearrange for work delivered: w = (h₁ − h₂) + (V₁² − V₂²)/2000 + g(z₁ − z₂)/1000 + q.
Kinetic term: V₁² = 3600 m²/s², V₂² = 22500 m²/s², difference = −18900 m²/s², so (V₁² − V₂²)/2000 = −18900/2000 = −9.45 kJ/kg.
Potential term: g(z₁ − z₂) = 9.81 × 5 = 49.05 J/kg = 0.049 kJ/kg.
Heat is lost, so q = −20 kJ/kg.
examples.answer: The turbine delivers w = 570.6 kJ/kg of steam, giving a power output of 1141.2 kW, about 1.14 MW.

traps: Dropping ΔKE in a nozzle, where it carries the answer, but keeping it in a turbine where it is a few kJ/kg against hundreds.
Adding V²/2 in J/kg straight to h in kJ/kg; use V²/2000 and gz/1000.
Wrong sign of w for a compressor: w is negative, and work input is h₂ − h₁, not h₁ − h₂.
Using u instead of h in a flow device. Flow work pv crosses with the mass; enthalpy is the correct energy per kg.
Writing h₁ = h₂ for a turbine because the casing is insulated. q = 0 does not mean h is constant; the enthalpy drop leaves as work.

quiz.q: Write the steady flow energy equation per unit mass and name every term with its unit.
quiz.a: h₁ + V₁²/2000 + gz₁/1000 + q = h₂ + V₂²/2000 + gz₂/1000 + w, with h in kJ/kg, V in m/s, z in m, g = 9.81 m/s², q heat added in kJ/kg and w work delivered in kJ/kg.

quiz.q: Why does the SFEE use enthalpy h and not internal energy u?
quiz.a: Mass crossing the boundary carries flow work pv with it: the fluid behind pushes it in and the fluid ahead pushes it out. Enthalpy h = u + pv bundles that flow work with the internal energy, so h is the energy per kg that actually enters and leaves a control volume.

quiz.q: Air flows through an insulated nozzle with h₁ = 3000 kJ/kg, V₁ = 50 m/s and h₂ = 2800 kJ/kg. Find V₂. Take Δz = 0.
A compressor takes in refrigerant at h₁ = 250 kJ/kg and delivers it at h₂ = 290 kJ/kg, with ṁ = 0.05 kg/s. Find the shaft power, ignoring KE and PE.
quiz.a: w = h₁ − h₂ = 250 − 290 = −40 kJ/kg. Negative means work is put in. Work input = 40 kJ/kg, so power input = 0.05 × 40 = 2 kW.

quiz.q: A throttle keeps h constant. Why does the temperature stay the same for an ideal gas but usually fall for a real gas?
quiz.a: For an ideal gas h depends on T alone, so h₁ = h₂ forces T₁ = T₂. For a real gas h depends on both T and p, so dropping the pressure at constant h shifts the temperature; this Joule-Thomson effect is what makes a throttle useful in a refrigerator.

quiz.q: In a turbine we ignore the kinetic energy term but in a nozzle we cannot. Justify both choices.
quiz.a: A turbine's enthalpy drop is hundreds of kJ/kg while the velocity change adds only a few kJ/kg, so dropping ΔKE changes the answer little. In a nozzle the whole point is to convert that enthalpy into velocity, and the velocity term becomes equal to the enthalpy drop — dropping it removes the answer.

quiz.q: Why is a pump's work input written as v(p₂ − p₁) rather than h₂ − h₁?
quiz.a: A liquid is nearly incompressible, so v stays constant and h₂ − h₁ = (u₂ − u₁) + v(p₂ − p₁). The temperature rise is tiny, so u₂ ≈ u₁ and the work input is v(p₂ − p₁); both forms are correct, the second is just easier.

beyond: Not for the exam. Steam-cycle designers combine the SFEE with turbine and pump maps; refrigeration engineers use the isenthalpic throttle as the standard expander. Exergy analysis in Unit 4 rates each term by how much work is truly available. Modern work extends to transient and multi-stream forms and to CFD, where h, V and z vary across a section. Search: control volume energy balance, flow work, Joule–Thomson coefficient, nozzle efficiency.
